t: Leetcodify Similar Friends — Verifying Friendship Pairs Against Co-Listening History
o: Report every friendship pair whose two users listened to at least three DIFFERENT songs on the SAME day, keeping the stored orientation user1_id < user2_id. In Example 1, users 1 and 2 are friends and both played songs 10, 11, 12 on 2021-03-15, so they are reported. Users 2 and 4 are friends but share only songs 10 and 11; users 2 and 5 are friends yet listened on different days — both excluded. Users 1 and 3 match musically but are NOT friends, so they are disqualified even though the recommendations problem would have paired them: here friendship is required, not forbidden. Duplicate listening rows mean the threshold must be checked against DISTINCT songs rather than raw rows.
k: Unlike friend recommendations, the friendship condition is mandatory, and output preserves the canonical user1_id < user2_id order from the Friendship table.
Count DISTINCT song ids per (pair, day) so duplicated listen rows cannot inflate the three-song bar.
A correlated EXISTS-style count per friendship row reads naturally; a grouped self-join plus semi-join shares aggregation work across all pairs at scale.

a.n: Approach 1: Correlated Count Per Friendship Row
a.i: Walk the Friendship table and, for each stored pair, count the distinct songs heard by BOTH users on the same day via a correlated inner join between their listening histories. Keep pairs whose count reaches three. The output columns come straight from Friendship, so the user1 < user2 orientation is preserved automatically.
s: Correlated subquery joins Listens a (user1) with Listens b (user2) on equal day and song_id.
Keep the friendship row when the count is at least 3.

c.python:
# LeetCode SQL problem - Python driver not applicable.
# SQL solution:
"""
SELECT f.user1_id,
       f.user2_id
FROM Friendship f
WHERE (
    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT a.song_id)
    FROM Listens a
    JOIN Listens b
      ON b.user_id = f.user2_id
     AND a.day = b.day
     AND a.song_id = b.song_id
    WHERE a.user_id = f.user1_id
) >= 3;
"""

a.t: O(F * L) — each of F friendship rows triggers a co-listen scan over the L-row log
a.sp: O(L) — join buffers for the correlated subquery

a.i: Compute qualifying pairs once: self-join Listens on matching day and song with l1.user_id < l2.user_id, group by (pair, day), and require COUNT(DISTINCT song_id) >= 3. Semi-joining that derived table back to Friendship keeps only real friendships and re-emits them in canonical column order, collapsing days via DISTINCT.
s: Self-join Listens l1/l2 on equal day and song_id restricted to l1.user_id < l2.user_id.
GROUP BY user pair and day; filter groups with HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT song_id) >= 3.
JOIN the result to Friendship on (user1_id, user2_id).
Apply SELECT DISTINCT so multiple qualifying days yield a single row per pair.

c.python:
# LeetCode SQL problem - Python driver not applicable.
# SQL solution:
"""
SELECT DISTINCT f.user1_id,
       f.user2_id
FROM Friendship f
JOIN (
    SELECT l1.user_id AS u1,
           l2.user_id AS u2,
           l1.day AS day,
           COUNT(DISTINCT l1.song_id) AS shared
    FROM Listens l1
    JOIN Listens l2
      ON l1.user_id < l2.user_id
     AND l1.day = l2.day
     AND l1.song_id = l2.song_id
    GROUP BY l1.user_id, l2.user_id, l1.day
    HAVING shared >= 3
) t ON f.user1_id = t.u1 AND f.user2_id = t.u2;
"""

a.t: O(L^2) — the self-join pairs co-listened rows before grouping prunes them
a.sp: O(L^2) worst case for the grouped intermediate table

w: The grouped self-join is the scalable form; the correlated query is fine for small tables and easiest to explain. Pitfalls: dropping the day from GROUP BY lets songs from separate days combine into a fake qualifying day; joining without the user_id < user2_id restriction doubles work; returning pairs in arbitrary orientations breaks the required output contract. Contrast with problem 1917 in an interview: identical mining logic, inverted friendship predicate, different output normalization. Follow-up: parameterize the threshold K shared songs, or weight matches by recency.
